activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: The squeal of microphone feedback happens when sound from a loudspeaker goes back into the microphone, gets amplified again, and loops louder and louder.
story:
Alexandra stood in the wings of the school auditorium, gripping her ukulele so hard her knuckles went white. Stage fright, her mother liked to say, was practically hereditary in their family, passed down like freckles. Alexandra didn't want to inherit it. In ten minutes she would play a solo in the spring concert, her first time on any stage, and the sound check had just gone horribly wrong.

She had watched it happen from the third row. Lex held the microphone at the front of the stage, and the moment Mr. Tanaka turned up the loudspeaker, a whistle tore through the room, sharp enough to make Kiera, sitting beside Alexandra, slap her hands over her ears. Mr. Tanaka shut everything off and stood there rubbing his chin.

Alexandra thought hard. The whistle had not started until the speaker was loud, and it had grown, louder and louder, as if something were feeding itself. She imagined the sound traveling: out of the loudspeaker, back into the microphone, then through the amplifier again, bigger each time, looping until it shrieked. The microphone and the speaker had to be pointed at each other. That was it, she decided, and she could test the idea. She climbed onto the stage, asked Lex to hold the mic exactly where he had before, and cupped her hands to feel where the speaker was aimed. Straight at him. She turned the speaker slightly toward the empty back wall, then nodded at Mr. Tanaka. "Try it now, but slowly."

The speaker came up, and Lex spoke into the microphone. No whistle. Kiera pumped both fists from the third row. "How did you know?" Mr. Tanaka asked, and Alexandra said, "The sound was looping back into the mic, so I sent it somewhere else."

Later, when the concert ended and the crowd cheered, the principal called her up again and read out a special citation for saving the sound check. Alexandra bowed, then leaned toward the microphone, which sat politely aimed away from every speaker in the building. "This one's for Lex," she whispered, "for standing there while I figured it out." From the front row, Lex shouted, "Anytime," and the whole auditorium laughed.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
Kaitlyn lined up six gummy bears on the kitchen table, each one labelled with a soaking time: zero minutes, ten, twenty, all the way up to fifty. She had chosen the project because gummy bears were made of a polymer, a stretchy, chewy stuff that soaked up water like a tiny sponge, and she wanted to know whether more time in water meant more growth. Her hypothesis, written neatly on an index card, said yes. Now she needed the numbers to back her up.

She measured each bear with a ruler and wrote the results in her notebook. The bear with zero minutes stayed two centimetres wide. The fifty-minute bear had swelled to almost three, and its edges had gone soft and blunted, as if the water were starting to erode them away. The pattern was clear: longer soaking, wider bear. Then she turned to her graph and got stuck.

Her friend Uriah came over after dinner to compare projects, and he spread his own graph on the table beside her bowl of soggy bears. "I graphed temperature on the up-and-down line," he said, "and plant height along the bottom." He frowned at it. Something looked wrong, and it took Kaitlyn a moment to see why. Her own graph had the same problem.

"Wait," she said slowly, tapping her pencil. "The thing I changed was the soaking time. The thing that changed because of it was the bear's width. The time should go along the bottom." She checked the page in her binder from Mr. Harper's class, and there it was, exactly as she remembered. "By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis." She read it aloud, then pulled her pencil across her paper. "The time I chose goes on x. The width I measured goes on y."

"That makes sense," Uriah said, already erasing his own axes. "My height depends on the temperature, so height is the dependent one. It goes up top." He redrew his lines while she redrew hers, and when both graphs were finished, they leaned over the table together. Kaitlyn's points climbed in a tidy diagonal, each dot a little higher than the last.

"Look at that," she said. "It actually worked." Uriah high-fived her, and one soggy gummy bear wobbled against the rim of the bowl.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
Zoey sat in the waiting room of Dr. Patel's office with her heart hammering, staring at a poster of bees that claimed a single bee can pollinate a whole field of flowers before lunchtime. The clock on the wall said 3:52. Her mother had to be back at work by 4:15, which meant Zoey had twenty-three minutes to get through the appointment she had been dreading for a week: her flu shot.

Sharon had come along because the two of them had planned to walk to the library after, and now Sharon was reading a note Zoey had passed her under the magazine rack. "You wrote me a letter?" Sharon whispered. "It's three sentences long." The note said: My anxiety is doing the thing again. I can't stop picturing the needle. Tell me what you do after a bad day, fast.

"Fast?" Sharon mouthed, but she scribbled back anyway. When the folded paper landed on Zoey's knee, she opened it. "Bad day plan," it read. "I run laps around my block until my legs are tired, then I go to bed early, like nine o'clock early, and I tell my brother everything even though he's annoying." Zoey read it twice. Exercise, sleep, and telling someone. She had spent the whole week instead lying on her bed with her curtains perpendicular to the window frame, fully closed, scrolling on her tablet and eating crackers. That, she realized, had not handled anything.

"Mr. Bondarenko calls that coping," Sharon whispered. "The ways you handle stress. He said it in gym after I bombed the mile run."

The nurse opened the door and called, "Zoey?" Zoey stood up so fast the magazine slid to the floor. She grabbed Sharon's hand, squeezed it once, and said, "Tonight, after this, we're running laps. Nine o'clock bedtime. And you're going to tell me everything, even the annoying parts."

"Deal," said Sharon. "Now go, your mom's watching the clock."

Zoey walked through the door before her anxiety could argue.

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: The contour interval is the difference in height between one contour line and the next, and it is printed in the map's legend.
story:
Juliette spread the topographic map across the library table, weighting the corners with books about volcanoes. Tommy dropped into the chair across from her and leaned over so far his nose almost touched the paper.

"Mr. Liu says the winner of Saturday's orienteering race gets to pick the prize," she said. "I want the compass, so we need to figure out which way up Hillside Park is the steepest before Tommy-from-the-other-team does."

"There's a Tommy on the other team?" Tommy said. "That's confusing."

"Focus." She traced a finger along one of the curly brown lines. "These are contour lines. Every line is the same height apart. So the steepest slope is wherever the lines crowd together, because you climb the same amount in way less distance."

Tommy counted the lines squished along the park's west edge. "Seven lines from bottom to top. That's like, seven times the height, right? That hill must be gigantic. My cousin's house is three stories and it only has stairs."

Juliette did some vigorous scribbling on her notepad. "If each line is fifty meters, that's three hundred and fifty meters. There's no way. I've climbed that hill. It took four minutes and I wasn't even tired." She frowned at the map. The hill was real, the lines were real, and the numbers refused to cooperate with her memory. Somewhere between paper and grass, something was wrong.

"You're assuming fifty," Lindsay said, sliding into the third chair with her hot chocolate. "You know what happens when you assume. You get wrong hills."

Juliette was about to argue, but instead she turned the map over, then checked the corners, then the bottom edge. There, in print so small she had to hold the paper under the desk lamp, was the legend. "Contour interval: 10 meters," she read aloud. "The difference in height between one contour line and the next. It's printed right there in the legend. I never even looked."

"So the hill is seventy meters," Tommy said, counting again. "Which is like a twenty-three-story building. Wait, no, I hate math."

"Seventy meters, and the steep part is still the west side, because that's where the lines bunch up no matter what the interval is." She tapped the tight cluster of lines. "We go up the west face and down the easy east side. Quick and brutal."

Lindsay raised her mug. "I'd toast to that, but the library charges a tariff if you spill, and I've already paid it twice this month."

They packed up at closing time. At the door, Juliette stopped and looked back at the map table, then at Tommy. "The other Tommy. Does he know about the legend?"

Tommy grinned and zipped his backpack shut. "He thinks the hill is three hundred and fifty meters tall. I heard him tell his whole team."

"Lindsay, forget the compass," Juliette said. "We're going to watch them climb nothing for an hour."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: On Buddhist observance days called uposatha, devout lay Buddhists may take eight precepts, including not eating after midday.
story:
The kitchen clock said 2:40, and Hailey's stomach growled so loudly that Zainab looked up from her homework. "Your grandma's not eating either," Zainab whispered, nodding toward the back door, where Hailey's grandmother was sweeping the porch with slow, even strokes. It was strange. Every Saturday of Hailey's life, the three of them had shared peanut butter cookies at the counter at exactly three o'clock, and Grandma had never once missed.

Hailey slid the cookie jar closer and peered through the window, watching the way Grandma moved, unhurried, like the sweeping itself was the whole point. "She took the precepts this morning," Hailey said slowly. "At the temple. She told Mom it's called uposatha, the observance day. She said the devout ones take eight precepts." She counted on her fingers, trying to be systematic about it. "Eight rules. And one of them must be the cookies, because she didn't touch breakfast either." Zainab raised an eyebrow. "You think a rule is about not eating?"

Instead of answering, Hailey took one cookie, broke it in half, and carried it out to the porch. "Grandma? Want some?" Grandma just smiled and shook her head, then pointed at the sky, where the sun had already passed its highest point. "Noon has gone, little one. Not until tomorrow." Hailey stood there holding the cookie while the pieces clicked into place: no food after midday, that was the pattern. That was why the temple aunties had packed away the lunch dishes so early, why nobody had touched the fruit basket all afternoon. She thought about how, an hour ago, she had complained to Mom that Grandma was being unfair by skipping their cookie time, and her ears went warm.

Back inside, she set the cookie halves on a plate and covered them with a bowl. "Tomorrow at three," she told Zainab. "She can have them tomorrow, after midday." Zainab grinned and stole one anyway, and through the window the sweeping kept its steady rhythm, shhh, shhh, like the sound of a very old dynasty of Saturday afternoons that had somehow, quietly, changed.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Alexandre spread his science fair notebook across the library table and groaned. "My project is doomed. Nobody will believe that store-brand cereal tastes the same as the fancy one, and I can't prove it."

Damien slid into the chair across from him, already chewing something. "Then prove it harder."

"That's the problem. Last week I asked my cousin which cereal she liked better, and she picked the one in the shiny box. Then she saw the price tags and changed her answer." Alexandre flipped to his data page, which had more crossed-out lines than a losing tic-tac-toe board. "People don't taste with their mouths. They taste with the box."

Mr. Qureshi, the librarian, paused his cart beside their table. "That's why some scientists hide the boxes," he said, shelving a book about lush rainforests on the shelf behind them, and rolled on before Alexandre could ask more.

Alexandre stared at the book, then at his notebook, then at Damien. "That's it. Nobody knows which bowl is which, so what they expect can't mess it up." He wrote the word BLIND in enormous letters. "We pour both cereals into plain bowls, label them A and B, and only I know which is which."

On Saturday they set up in the library meeting room. Chris went first, sampling each bowl with the seriousness of a judge. "B. Definitely B." B was the store brand, the cheap one, the one Chris had always accused of tasting like cardboard.

Alexandre tested nine more people. Seven picked the store brand, including Damien, who had begged his mom for the name-brand box every single week for a year.

When Alexandre tallied the final column, Damien leaned over his shoulder and read the answer key. He went quiet for a long moment.

"So all those Saturday mornings I did extra chores," he said slowly, "for cardboard."

Alexandre grinned and circled his conclusion. "Want to be subject number eleven? We still have half a box of A left."

Damien picked up the spoon.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
story:
The lights went out all at once, and Arthur's half-finished equation for math homework vanished from his screen. He waited in the dark, counting seconds, but nothing hummed back on. Through the window he could see that the whole street was black, porch lights and all, so he grabbed a flashlight and went out to the backyard where his dad was already standing.

"Look up," his dad said.

Arthur did, and then he couldn't stop looking. The sky wasn't the usual handful of stars. A pale, grainy river of light ran across the darkness, thick in places, thin in others, like something spilled. He had never seen that from home, not once in twelve years.

Flavie climbed over the low fence from next door, with Shayla right behind her. Shayla insisted the pale river was a cloud, and Flavie insisted it was the Milky Way, and their voices climbed until Arthur held up both hands. "Let's settle it instead of arguing," he said, mediating before it turned into a real fight. "Stars twinkle. Clouds don't. Watch the edge of it for a minute." They watched, and the light shimmered, thousands of tiny points, unmistakably stars. Flavie pumped her fist.

"But why can't we see it every night?" Shayla asked. "It's right there."

Arthur remembered a poster from the library, the numbers stuck in his head because they had surprised him. "It said about 80 percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light," he said. "All our porch lights and streetlights, they wash it out." Tonight the power cut had shut every one of those lights off at once, and the sky had answered.

"Like the stars were always waiting," Flavie said. A flock of geese crossed overhead, dark shapes following the river of light south, and Shayla pointed up at them, tracking the birds until the last one passed.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
story:
Mason pulled his cleats from his locker and found Ally already sitting on the bench, glove on her knee, dressed for baseball tryouts. He blinked. "You're trying out? There's no girls' baseball team here."

"That's kind of the point," Ally said, tying her laces. "I want to know why there isn't one."

Mason chewed on that while he changed. It seemed like a strange thing to wonder about. Teams just existed, or they didn't, like weather. But if there was no girls' team, then a girl who wanted to play had only one option, and Ally was taking it. That was a pattern you could see, and patterns usually had something behind them. He wondered what.

Mr. Eze, the coach, came through the locker room counting heads. He stopped at Ally. "You lost, sweetheart? Softball sign-ups are in the gym."

"I'm here for baseball," Ally said. "I checked the rules. There's a law, Title IX, signed in 1972. It bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. Our school gets federal money, right? And it's been applied to sports programs."

Mr. Eze rubbed his jaw. "We've never had a girl try out."

"Well," Ally said, "now you do."

Mason couldn't stop himself. "So if the school doesn't offer girls' baseball," he said slowly, working it out aloud, "then you get to try out for ours. That follows." He turned the idea over. A coach couldn't just say no because of her category; the law made sex an illegal factor in the decision. The only factors left would be speed, arm, glove, swing. It was almost like a puzzle where one cause was hidden and Ally had just named it.

But Mason liked testing things. "Hypothetical," he said to Mr. Eze. "Say you cut her today, before she even catches a ball. That would be deciding based on what, exactly?"

Mr. Eze looked at Mason for a long moment. "Based on nothing," he said finally. "Get on the field, both of you."

Tryouts ran long. Ally dropped one ball in the outfield but threw a strike to home that buzzed past Mason's ear, and her swing was short and quick. When the list went up on the locker room door the next afternoon, Mason pushed through the crowd and ran his finger down the names. His was there. And there, four lines below, was hers.

He found her at her locker and tapped the paper. "You made it."

"Figured as much," Ally said, but she was grinning as she stuffed her glove into her bag.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: Lifting the head forward to breathe makes the hips and legs sink, adding drag; turning the head to the side keeps the body flat.
story:
Arianna hung the orange traffic cone on the fence post at the far end of the pool and stared at it. Twenty-five metres, the coach had said, front crawl, with side breathing, tomorrow at tryouts or nothing else. Tomorrow. She pushed off into the backyard water and counted her strokes, and every single time she needed air she lifted her face forward toward the cone, gulped, and put her face back down.

"You look like a windmill falling over," called Madina from the lawn chair, her view of the far end partly obstructed by the big hydrangea. "Your feet keep vanishing."

"That's the shallow end shelf," Arianna said, but she knew it wasn't. Twice more she swam, and twice more her legs dragged lower and lower until her kick churned up white water and she stopped, gasping. The water felt heavy, like it was grabbing her shins. She hauled herself out and sat on the concrete, the strap of her goggles pressing painfully on the stiff cartilage of her ear, and watched Madina float calmly on her back, barely moving, barely sinking at all.

Arianna thought hard. Her legs didn't sink while she was gliding. They sank when she breathed. Something about lifting her head forward was doing it, like her body was a seesaw and her face was the heavy end going up. She turned to Madina. "Watch me. This time I'm going to turn my head sideways instead of up, just enough to get air. Aggressive kick, same as before, nothing else changed."

She pushed off, counted three strokes, and turned her cheek toward the sky instead of her whole face. One quick breath, mouth at the corner, face back in the water. Her legs stayed up near the surface, almost flat. She touched the far wall and looked back, open-mouthed, at how short the wake behind her was.

Madina was on her feet. "Do it again!"

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
Alexa sat cross-legged on her bed with her notebook open, because something strange had been happening and she wanted to figure it out. Every Sunday night, her stomach knotted up like a twisted intestine, and by Monday morning she felt sick enough to miss school sometimes, but never on Saturdays. She had drawn a little calendar in the notebook and marked every bad-stomach day with an X, and the X's made a pattern: Sundays, over and over. Was it something she ate? She budgeted her snacks carefully for a week, nothing greasy after lunch, and the Sunday knot came anyway. So it probably was not the food.

She flopped back against her pillow and called Kristopher on her tablet, because he had missed a whole month of school last year and she wanted to ask him something. "Remember when you were out forever?" she said. "What was actually wrong? Was it your stomach?"

He nodded on the screen, his bedroom door shut behind him. "It started out as stomach stuff, yeah. My mom thought it was trivial at first, like nerves before a test. But it got really intense and it lasted months, and I could not go to school or anything. The doctor said when anxiety is that bad and it gets in the way of your life, they can diagnose an anxiety disorder." He shrugged. "It is treatable. I talked to the doctor, and it got way better after that."

Alexa wrote anxiety disorder in her notebook and underlined it twice. "So feeling anxious sometimes is just normal? But when it is huge and sticks around and blocks everything, that is when it becomes a disorder?" Her Sunday knot suddenly made sense in a way snacks never had.

"That is what they told me," Kristopher said. "Also the doctor gave me coping stuff, like breathing exercises and setting boundaries on things that stressed me out."

Alexa tried one right there, breathing in for four counts and out for six, and the tight feeling in her chest loosened just a little. She wrote coping at the top of a fresh page. "I'm going to track the breathing all week," she said, "and see if the Sunday X's shrink. And I'm telling my mom tonight, so she can call the doctor."

"Good plan," Kristopher said.

Alexa picked up her pencil and drew, at the bottom of the calendar, one small square with no X in it yet.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: A bylaw is a rule made by a local government, such as a city or town council, and it applies only within that municipality.
story:
Elena had signed up to speak at the town hall meeting because of the skate park. The park was ten minutes from her house, and the sign at the gate said no skateboards after 4 p.m. She and her friends had been kicked out twice, once in the middle of a run.

She was third on the speaker list. While she waited, she practiced her speech on Japji, who had come along to hold her note cards. "I used to think the rule was some big national law," Elena whispered. "Then I looked it up. It's a bylaw. That means it's a rule made by our town council, and it only applies inside our own town."

"Only here?" Japji said.

"Only inside this municipality," Elena said. "In Greenfield, ten kilometres away, the park stays open until nine."

When her name was called, she walked to the microphone. She said who she was, said the after-school ban pushed riders onto the streets where cars turned in, and asked the council to change the hours. A man at the far table, Mr. Rowe, leaned toward his microphone and said the ban had been requested by neighbours who complained about noise, and that noise complaints were subjective, so the council had to guess where to draw the line.

Elena had prepared for exactly this. "You don't have to guess," she said. "Greenfield changed its bylaw last year. You could call their office and ask what happened after. If complaints went down, that's evidence, not a guess." She also asked how a citizen could formally request a change, and Mr. Rowe told her: gather signatures on a petition and bring it to any councillor, who could then put the bylaw amendment on a council agenda. He said most petitions started with fewer names than people expected. "Councillors respond to numbers on paper," he said. "That's the part citizens forget."

The council chair thanked her and moved to the next speaker, a woman arguing about a stop sign. Elena sat back down, and Japji passed her the note cards she had crushed in her fist.

Afterward, Mr. Rowe caught her by the door. "You made a decent inference up there," he said. "Greenfield did change its hours, and complaints did drop. I know because I called them two weeks ago." He paused. "The reason I bring it up is that your name is on a petition that reached my desk this morning. Your brother started it at the skate park. Ninety-two signatures."

Elena stared at him. Her brother had told her he was going to the meeting to sit in the back row.

"He's waiting outside," Mr. Rowe said. "He wanted you to find out from me. I'd say that makes you even for the time he put your skateboard on the roof."

Elena pushed through the double doors, and there he stood, holding the clipboard, with Japji's little sister already adding her name.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
story:
Scarlett spread her pencils across the library table like a surgeon laying out tools. Today she would finish her drawing of the old oak behind the library, with its shadowed trunk and glossy leaves, and enter it in the library's summer art contest. Brady leaned over from the next chair, chewing a straw.

"Your tree looks like it's made of fog," he said.

Scarlett held up her sketch. He was right. Every line came out pale gray, so faint the paper seemed to camouflage the drawing, the trunk vanishing right into the white. She had traced over the shadow side three times and it still looked like a whisper.

She thought back to last Saturday, when Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya, the librarian, had shown the class the art supply cabinet. "Take care of the pencils," he had warned, "or they'll take care of you." She remembered digging through the box fast, grabbing whatever her fingers found, because Brady was racing her to the window seats. She hadn't looked at a single label.

Now she scrutinized the pencil in her hand. On the end, tiny letters: 4H. She lined up the others. 2B. HB. 6B. A pattern was hiding in those letters, she could feel it. She flipped the pencils, squinting, then pulled Michaela over from the graphic novel shelf.

"Read this. What's it say?"

"6B," said Michaela. "And that one's 4H. My grandpa says H means hardness and B means blackness."

Blackness. Scarlett's heart did a somersault. She snatched the 6B and drew one swooping branch. The mark came out rich and velvety dark, like the tree had finally shown up in person.

"Brady. Brady. Look at this branch."

He scrutinized it with the straw still in his mouth. "Okay, that tree means business."

She filled the whole shadow side in minutes, the pencil gliding soft and deep, and the oak grew so bold and eloquent that two kids at the next table leaned sideways to see it. When Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya passed by, he stopped.

"Now that," he said, "is a tree with opinions."

Scarlett grinned and wrote her name at the bottom in 6B.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: If milk costs 2.65 and you pay with 5.00, the correct change is 2.35, whatever the currency.
story:
Samuel's mother put five dollars and an empty cloth bag on the kitchen table, which felt like being handed the keys to a rocket. "Milk, two percent, and come straight back," she said. "I'll be here." She did not say the word supervise, but she stood at the window in a way that said it anyway.

At the corner store, Samuel found the milk, checked the tag twice, and read it to himself like a password: two dollars and sixty-five cents. He carried it to the counter, where Madelyn from his science class was stacking gum. "You're buying milk alone?" she said. "Very influential of you. Next you'll be driving."

He handed over the five-dollar bill. The cashier gave him back a toonie, a quarter, and a dime. Samuel stepped aside so the man behind him could pay, and only then did he count it in his palm. Two dollars and thirty-five cents was what he should have. He counted again, slower, and got two dollars and thirty-five again, which was wrong, because the quarter plus the dime was only thirty-five, and with the coin he was holding, that made two thirty-five, and two thirty-five from five was right, so wait. He frowned at his own hand like it was a puzzle box.

Then he saw it. The cashier had given him two dollars and thirty-five cents, and the milk cost two sixty-five, and five minus two sixty-five was exactly two thirty-five. It was right. He had been so sure he'd be cheated that he'd almost cheated himself.

Back in the kitchen, he set the milk on the table and counted the change out loud, coin by coin, ending with the dime. "Two sixty-five plus two thirty-five is five," he said. "Exactly five."

His mother looked at the little heap of coins and then at him. "And your diagnosis of the trip?"

"Success," Samuel said. "One thing, though. Madelyn thinks walking to the store alone makes me influential. I think it just makes me thirsty." He picked up the carton, shook it once, and went to find a glass.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
The bus smelled like wet jackets and banana peel, and Luca was losing an argument, which was the worst place to lose one. "Devon Marsh is the best player in the league," Edmond said, holding up his phone. "It says so. He's ranked number one." Luca looked at the screen. One number, next to one name, like that settled everything. "He scores the most goals," Luca said slowly, "but half of them were when the other team had their backup goalie in." Ava leaned over the seat. "Then prove it."

That was the problem. Proving it meant showing something you couldn't see just by watching, the way you couldn't see wind, only the branches moving. Luca wanted to conquer the whole ranking with facts, not just yell louder than Edmond. At dinner that night he complained about it, and his uncle laughed. "You know what you're talking about is an old trick," he said. "There's a book called Moneyball, from 2003, by Michael Lewis. It described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players. A low-budget team using numbers to find players nobody else wanted." Luca wrote on-base percentage on his hand, because his notebook was upstairs and ideas were brittle things, easily lost.

The next morning he brought a crumpled sheet of paper onto the bus. He had gone through the league site and counted, for eight players, how often each one helped keep a possession alive, passes that reached a teammate, recoveries, the small stuff that never made the highlights. "Marsh is ranked first on goals," he told Edmond, "but look. When he's on the field, his team keeps the ball less. When Ramon plays, they keep it more. The ranking is one number squeezed out of a hundred things." Ava frowned at the paper. "You counted all that?" "Twice," Luca said. "The second time because I didn't believe the first."

Edmond didn't give in right away, which was fair, because one crumpled page against a whole official ranking looked ridiculous. But the coach had posted a ballot on the gym door that week, voting for the league all-star team, and Ava had an idea. "Let people vote before the game and after," she said. "Not for goals. For who you'd want on your team if you had to win one game."

Luca watched the votes come in after Saturday's match, Marsh's name circled over and over, and his stomach dropped. Then the coach sorted them, and there was the twist: the kids who had actually played against Ramon's team had written his name, almost every single one, because they had spent forty minutes chasing the ball and never getting it. The kids who hadn't played had voted for Marsh.

Edmond stared at the two piles for a long moment. "So the ranking is like a poll of people who never played him," he said. Luca folded his page into a careful square and put it in his pocket. "Ramon's buying the pizza," Ava announced. "New rule, and I'm not taking votes."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
Emmett slid into the back seat of the car and angled the visor mirror so he could see his chin. Three new spots had appeared overnight, red and obvious, like they had appointed themselves to his face without asking.

"Picture day is in forty minutes," his mom said from the driver's seat. "I'm dropping you and Zayn at school, then I've got to get to work."

Zayn climbed in beside him, took one look, and said, "It's getting worse, huh."

"Thanks for the update." Emmett tilted his chin toward the window, then back. "It started exactly one week after school began. I counted. Zero pimples all summer, then a whole tsunami of them in September. That's a pattern, right? Something changed."

"Maybe it's the school soap," Zayn said.

"I used the same soap all summer." Emmett pulled up a search on his phone, scrolling fast. "It says here hormones in puberty make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil, and that oil is called sebum." He read the next line under his breath, then out loud. "The sebum can clog your pores, and clogged pores lead to acne. So it's not the soap. It's under the skin. The stuff causing this is invisible."

"So what do we do about it?"

"There's a pharmacy two blocks from school." Emmett leaned forward between the seats. "Mom, can we stop? Ten minutes, I promise. There's supposed to be face wash that helps."

"We have twenty minutes before photos. That's cutting it close." She signaled and turned anyway. "Ten minutes. Not eleven."

At the pharmacy, Emmett found the skin aisle and grabbed the first bottle he saw, but a girl his age was already there, holding two different face washes side by side, turning them over. He hesitated, then just asked. "Does yours say anything about oil?"

She showed him a label. "This one says it unclogs pores. That's the whole problem, right? Puberty hormones make your skin pump out more oil, sebum or whatever, and it blocks everything up." She pointed at a second bottle. "This one just says gentle. That's not very explicit about what it actually does."

Emmett read both labels himself, comparing. The pore one named the exact problem he had. He took it to the register with his own allowance money, and they ran two blocks to school with the bottle rattling in his backpack.

In the gym line for photos, he ducked into the washroom and scrubbed his chin, careful and thorough, the way the label's directions said. It wouldn't fix the spots in five minutes, and he knew that. But the cause had a name now, and a bottle, and a plan, and that felt like a whole different thing than last week.

"Emmett, you're up," called Mr. Le, who was herding kids in front of the camera.

Emmett wiped his hands on his jeans and stepped onto the mark. He thought of the label in his bag, took a breath, and lifted his chin.

"Smile," said the photographer.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
story:
Alexandra had just pulled a nutritious dinner of leftover noodles out of the microwave when every light in the house went dark, the fridge stopped humming, and the whole street outside the window turned into a row of unlit boxes. Her phone showed eleven percent battery, which meant she had maybe fifteen minutes to figure out what happened before she lost her only flashlight-that-could-also-call-people. That was the deadline, and she set it like homework: solve the mystery before the phone died.

First she tried the obvious answers. She checked the fuse box with a real flashlight, which was fine. She looked out front and saw that the neighbours' houses were dark too, so it wasn't just her house acting up. Then she noticed the irony of the situation: the one room with a working light was her fish tank, which ran on a battery-powered backup lamp, and its glow kept flickering as the power seemed to fluctuate, sometimes surging faintly, sometimes nothing at all. Flickering like that meant electricity was still coming down the line somewhere. Something was interrupting it partway along, and partway along, she remembered, was the big maple at the corner of Willow's street.

She texted Willow: "Is your power out? Check your window but DO NOT go outside. Something might be down on the wire by the maple. Tell me what you see, then ask your mom to call it in." Three dots, then: "Power out here too. I can see a WIRE across the sidewalk from my window!! A branch fell on it. Mom is calling the power company NOW." Alexandra sent back one more line, burning her last two percent: "Good. It's not sparking but that doesn't matter. A fallen line can still be live even when it looks dead, so nobody goes near it until they say it's safe."

The phone went black right after she hit send, and she sat in the fish tank's blue glow, eating cold noodles and feeling oddly proud of a mystery solved in the dark. Twenty minutes later a repair truck's yellow lights swept the ceiling, and boots crunched up the walk. A worker knocked twice and called through the door, "Power's coming back in ten, folks. And hey, somebody reported that downed line on Maple Street exactly right. Kept everybody clear of it. That was some smart kid."

From the window, Alexandra raised her cold-noodle fork in salute.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: In an ordered pair like (3, 5), the first number tells how far to move across along the x-axis and the second tells how far to move up or down.
story:
The note taped to the corner store's freezer door said, "SWEET TOOTH HUNT: solve the equations, plot the points, find the prize," and below it Ms. Rahimi had written two equations, 2x + 3 = 11 and 3y - 1 = 14, plus a grid. Michael stared at it while the fog on the glass slowly evaporated, because solving for x was easy, x equals 4, and solving for y was easy too, y equals 5. The problem was the grid. He had to plot (4, 5), and he had no idea which number went across and which went up.

Ryerson leaned over his shoulder, chewing a licorice twist. "Just pick one. It's random anyway. Across, up, who cares?"

"It's not random," Michael said. "Ms. Rahimi hid something at one spot. If I put the point in the wrong place, I'll be searching under the wrong shelf all afternoon."

Emanuel pushed between them, breathless from the run over. "My sister and I fight about this all the time. We play battleship on graph paper and she swears (3, 5) means go up three first, then across five. She wins every single time, too, which is the worst part."

Michael stopped chewing his own licorice. "She wins every time. So she's doing something right." He borrowed Ms. Rahimi's marker from the cup by the register, held it over the grid, and tried Emanuel's sister's way, up first. His dot landed on the spot for (5, 3), which the map labeled as the cat food aisle. He looked at the map's little legend again, and there it was in small print: the first number tells how far to move across, and the second tells how far to move up or down. He wiped the dot away with his sleeve and slid the marker across four, then up five. The point landed on the magazine rack by the window.

All three of them walked over, trying to look casual, which fooled nobody. Behind a stack of car magazines sat a jar with a folded paper inside. Michael opened it and read it out loud: "One free slushie, any size. Also, one citation for Excellent Mathematics, signed, Ms. Rahimi."

"A citation?" Ryerson said. "Like from the police?"

"Like from a teacher," Ms. Rahimi called from behind the register, not looking up from her crossword. "It's an award. I give one out every month, and nobody has won it since spring." She pointed her pen at Michael. "You're the first person all year to plot the point correctly. The last kid dug through the cat food for twenty minutes."

Emanuel laughed so hard he had to lean on the freezer door. "I have to tell my sister. She's going to be insufferable."

Michael tucked the citation into his back pocket, ordered the largest slushie the machine could make, and raised the cup toward the magazine rack like a toast.

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: Subtext is what a character means or feels beneath the words they actually say, and actors often show it through pauses, tone and gesture.
story:
The community theatre was so dilapidated that rain dripped into a bucket near the front row, but Grace loved it anyway. She had auditioned for the youth showcase and won a monologue about a girl whose family was moving away. The trouble was the lines. "I'm fine," the girl says three times. "I'm fine, really. I'm fine." Delivered flat, they meant nothing at all.

"That's the point," said Matis, who was running the spotlight from the booth. "Mr. Fraser calls it subtext. It's what she means or feels underneath what she's actually saying." Grace chewed on that while Adrien read the other parts from a folding chair on stage. She tried shouting the lines, then crying them, and both sounded fake. That night she drafted three different versions in her notebook, one for each "I'm fine," but she still couldn't figure out how an audience would know the girl wasn't fine if the words kept insisting she was.

In the morning she watched Adrien and Matis argue about who had eaten the last of the donuts, and she noticed something. When Adrien said "I don't care," his shoulders dropped and he looked at the empty box for a beat too long. He cared plenty. The pause told her, and so did his hands, which hovered near the box as if he wanted to close it gently. Grace grabbed her script. The words could stay exactly the same while everything around them changed.

At rehearsal she stood centre stage and tried it. "I'm fine," she said, and paused, folding and unfolding a tissue. "I'm fine, really," softer, glancing at an imaginary moving truck through the wings. The third one she said to the ceiling, not to anyone, with one hand pressed flat against her stomach. Mr. Fraser stopped shuffling his papers. Matis leaned out of the booth. "Whatever you just did," Adrien called from the dark, "do it exactly like that on Saturday." Grace tucked the tissue into her pocket, where she could find it again.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In traditional Chinese culture white is worn for mourning at funerals, while in many Western weddings the bride wears white.
story:
Isla slid her sketchbook under the mashed potatoes just as her dad set down the chicken. "We have a wardrobe emergency," he announced. "Your great-aunt Fiona is getting remarried on Saturday, and Uncle Dai's memorial is Sunday. Two events, one weekend."

"Two outfits," Isla's mom said, already cutting chicken. "Wear the navy to the memorial and something bright to the wedding."

"The problem," her dad said, "is that Isla only owns one nice dress. The white one with the strawberries."

Isla pulled the sketchbook back out. "So I wear it to the wedding. Brides wear white. That's the whole point." She had drawn the dress that afternoon, adding pockets, because real dresses should have pockets.

"Not to this wedding," her mom said. "Fiona's marrying into the Lin family. Uriah's family, actually. His grandmother will be there."

Isla put down her fork. "What's wrong with white at a wedding?"

Her mom shrugged. "Ask Uriah. I only know it's a thing."

After dinner, Isla called him. Uriah picked up on the second ring, with chewing sounds in the background.

"Quick question," she said. "Can I not wear white to Fiona's wedding because of your grandmother?"

There was a pause, then a laugh that sounded like a cough. "In traditional Chinese culture, white is what you wear to mourn someone at a funeral. My grandma would see a girl in white at a wedding and think somebody died."

"At a funeral? White?"

"At funerals," Uriah said. "Meanwhile your brides wear white and it means the opposite thing. My cousin thinks this is hilarious. She calls it a color war."

Isla sat on her bed and looked at the strawberry dress hanging on the closet door. Same color, two meanings, depending on who was looking. It was like her brother's algorithm for rock-paper-scissors: the same throw won or lost depending on the other side. She needed more information about the other side.

"Uriah, is there a color that means nothing bad to anyone?"

"Red," he said immediately. "Red is the luckiest color we have. Wear red and my grandmother will probably try to feed you extra dumplings."

Isla owned nothing red. She owned the white dress, a gray hoodie, and a pair of overalls she'd decorated with markers during a rebellious phase in fourth grade. She texted Cameron, who had a red sweater shaped like a giant strawberry. Cameron agreed to trade for the weekend but demanded the marker overalls as collateral, to "preserve for history."

Saturday arrived. Isla walked into the reception in Cameron's sweater, feeling like a stop sign. Uriah's grandmother spotted her from across the room, elbowed three relatives aside, and steered her toward the dumpling table.

"Red," the grandmother said, nodding firmly. "Good girl."

She piled a plate so high that Isla had to hold it with both hands. Uriah grinned from behind the tea kettle.

"Told you," he said. "Extra dumplings. You passed the color war."

"Tell her the sweater's a rental," Isla whispered. "If she feeds me any more, Cameron's getting it back stretched."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
story:
Jaxson sat at the kitchen table with a box of tissues, a bowl of unfinished soup, and a nose that would not open no matter how many times he blew. He had blown so hard that his ears popped. He counted the used tissues, eleven, and his nose still felt like a cork was stuck in it. That made no sense. If the problem was mucus, and he kept removing mucus, the blockage should be gone.

His laptop sat beside the soup, open to a message from Wassim: We have to nominate someone for class rep tomorrow, so hurry up and get better. Are you still voting for Alyvia? Jaxson typed back one-fingered, since he could only breathe through his mouth. He had promised Alyvia his vote because she'd promised to push for a longer lunch, and he wasn't changing his mind. Then, out of pure frustration, he typed his actual problem into the search bar: why does my nose stay blocked after blowing it.

He read the result twice. His nose felt stuffed mainly because of swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only a buildup of mucus. He stared at the screen. So all that blowing had been like bailing water out of a boat while the hole was somewhere else. If the swelling was the real culprit, maybe steam would reach it. It was worth a test.

He carried the soup to the stove, turned the burner back on, and leaned over the rising steam with a towel over his head like a tent. Slowly, one nostril cracked open, then a little more. He laughed, which made him cough, which was still somehow the best he'd felt all day.

Wassim messaged again: Did you die? Jaxson typed back with both hands, breathing through his nose while he did it. "Still alive. Nose half open. Voting for Alyvia, and tomorrow I'm going to tell Ms. Dhillon her homework was wrong." He took another slow breath and leaned back over the pot.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
story:
Alexis laced his skates in the loud hallway outside the rink and noticed that his hands felt slow on the strings. He had stayed up until two in the morning playing a racing game, and now his whole body seemed to be answering him a half second late. On the bench across from him, Aleksandar was bouncing his knees, wide awake.

"You look like a zombie," Aleksandar said.

"I feel like a zombie," Alexis said. He tried a crossovers drill on the warm-up lap and clipped the cone twice. Ms. Mensah, who ran the tryouts, blew her whistle and told everyone to participate in the passing drill in their assigned lanes. Alexis dropped a pass that landed right on his stick.

During a water break, Charlotte sat down beside him at the boards. "You were fine at the skills camp last week," she said. "What's different?"

Alexis thought about it. Same skates, same rink, same drills. The only thing different was the night before. He remembered a poster in the school nurse's office, the one he had read while waiting for a bandage. It said sleep experts recommend nine to twelve hours of sleep a night for kids aged six to twelve, and eight to ten for teenagers. He had counted on his fingers: if he had to get up at seven, and he was eleven, he should have been asleep by ten at the latest. Two in the morning had left him with five hours.

"I think I know what it is," Alexis said. "I got five hours of sleep. Kids our age are supposed to get nine to twelve. Even teenagers only need as little as eight, but I'm not a teenager, and I didn't even get that."

"Test it," Charlotte said. "Go to bed early tonight and see."

"Tonight's no good," Alexis said. "There's no second tryout." But there was a second half of the tryout, right now, and his body was still the same body. He could not fix five hours with a water break. He decided to change what he could: stop trying to be fast and start being early. If his reactions were slow, he would position himself where the puck was about to be. He stopped chasing the play and began drifting to the open lane, and two passes arrived exactly where he was standing. His shot went in off the post.

Ms. Mensah checked her clipboard. "Nice read, Alexis. That's hockey sense."

At the end, she posted the list on the glass by the door. Alexis made the practice squad. Aleksandar made it too and immediately began describing his plan to sell custom stick tape to the team, since he had decided he was an entrepreneur now.

"Tape costs four dollars," Charlotte said. "You're charging six."

"Two dollars for convenience," Aleksandar said. "That's called business."

Alexis pulled out his phone and set a bedtime alarm for ten o'clock. He labeled it "9 to 12 hours" and showed it to Aleksandar, whose bedtime alarm was already set for eleven thirty.

"That's not enough," Alexis said. "You're twelve, not a teenager."

"Eight to ten," Aleksandar said with a groan, and changed it to ten.

They walked out through the abrupt cold of the rink doors into the parking lot, skates swinging from their shoulders. "Rematch tomorrow," Alexis said. "Well-rested and faster."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Egyptian farmers used a shaduf, a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy weight on the other, to lift river water up to their fields.
story:
Hudson's worksheet had one question left: why did ancient Egyptians build the pyramids, and how did the Nile shape their farming? The answer had to come from the exhibit, and the exhibit was a hallway of glass cases holding things that refused to talk. His partner Daria had her own plan, which was to finish first and get to the gift shop before the bus left. "You read, I'll signal if I find anything," she said, holding up her hand like a referee.

The pyramid part came quickly enough. The floods made the land rich, the farmers grew extra grain, and extra grain fed the workers who stacked the stones. Hudson wrote that down. The farming part was harder. A painting showed fields higher than the river, green rows up on a bank, and he could not figure out how water got up there. Rivers went downhill. That was a rule, like gravity, which he had personally tested off the garage roof.

Daria found the case before he did. Inside was a long pole mounted on a post, with a bucket hanging on one end and a heavy stone lashed to the other. The label said one word: shaduf. "It's called a shaduf," Daria read, then wandered off toward the mugs.

Hudson stayed. The pole was tilted, bucket low, stone high. If a farmer pulled the bucket down into the river, the stone went up. Then the stone came down, and the bucket rose, and the water rose with it, up to the fields on the bank. The Nile flooded, but only part of the year; the rest of the year the water sat below the fields, and this lever hauled it up bucket by bucket. Nobody could see the river doing this over three thousand years, any more than you could see a log decompose into dirt in the dirt itself, but the tool was the evidence. He wrote it all out, feeling impartial about his own handwriting for once.

On the bus, Daria leaned over. "Okay, yours was better. What did it say?" Hudson turned the worksheet so she could see, and pointed at the drawing he had added in the margin, a pole, a bucket, and a stone, tilted and ready to lift.

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: Hamlet's famous speech beginning 'To be, or not to be' is a soliloquy in Act 3, Scene 1 of Shakespeare's play.
story:
Benjamin stood at the edge of the school auditorium stage, script crumpled in one fist, and tried again. "To be, or not to be," he said, all in one breath, rushing the words like a kid reciting for the fire drill. Ms. Campbell-Brown had assigned everyone a monologue for the spring showcase, and Benjamin wanted his to be the best one, the one people clapped extra for.

From the third row, Rudy cupped his hands around his mouth. "You're doing the most famous speech in the whole world. Slow down, man."

"It's famous," Benjamin called back, "so I have to do it big." He spread his arms wide, which felt heroic for about two seconds and then just felt silly. Otis, up in the lighting booth, flicked a spotlight on and off to show he agreed with Rudy.

At the drama club meeting that afternoon, Benjamin found the class copy of the play and flipped through it, hunting. Rudy leaned over his shoulder. "What are you looking for?"

"Where my speech lives," Benjamin said. "It can't be random. If it's famous, it sits somewhere important." He ran his finger down the page and stopped. "Here. It's in Act 3, Scene 1."

Rudy frowned. "So?"

"So it's not the beginning and it's not the end. It's a soliloquy in the middle of everything, right in Act 3, Scene 1. A guy alone on stage in the middle of the play." Benjamin tried the line again, quieter this time. "To be," he said, and let the pause stretch out, "or not to be." The empty auditorium seemed to hold its breath with him.

"Better," Rudy whispered.

"It's like he's in a negotiation with himself," Benjamin said slowly, "and he's trying to conceal which side is winning." He lifted one hand, hesitated, let it drop.

For the audition on Friday, Benjamin walked to center stage, took his time, and made the pause so long that even Otis in the booth stopped fiddling with the lights. Then he spoke.

"Can I try out with a speech nobody's ever heard of?" Rudy asked afterward. "That Hamlet one is notorious. It's everywhere."

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: Hula kahiko, the older style of Hawaiian hula, is danced to chanting and traditional instruments such as gourd drums rather than to sung melodies.
story:
Emile stood barefoot on his aunt's lanai, moving his feet the way he had practiced all week, and every time he did, the dance fell apart. In two days the whole neighborhood would gather at the park for the festival, and his aunt's halau had agreed that he could dance with them, if he could keep time.

He had assumed the problem was his feet. Last night he remembered something from that first rehearsal, when he'd stood at the back watching everybody. He had hummed the tune in his head, the kind of melody you hear on the radio, and his steps had drifted ahead of the group. But the older dancers weren't following any melody at all. The sound came from a hollowed gourd drum that one woman thumped against the floor, and from the chant, low and steady, rising out of the dancers themselves. Nobody was singing anything you could hum.

So he tried an experiment. He shut his eyes, ignored his feet completely, and listened only to the drumbeat and the chant words. When the gourd struck, his heel touched down; when the chant's syllables stretched, his hands rose to symbolize the wind over the mountain. It worked. The dance hung on the sound instead of on a tune, and his steps landed where they were supposed to land. He tried it again with the recording his aunt had played, the same chant, the same drum, and the timing stayed consistent, beat after beat.

The lanai tiles were cold through the thin mat, though the afternoon air was warm, the sort of insulation from heat he was glad of after an hour of practice. He texted Paisley, who had offered to play ukulele for him. "Can't be a song," he wrote. "It's hula kahiko, the old style. It goes with chanting and the gourd drum, not a melody." He had told her yesterday he'd need music, and he'd been wrong, and it felt strange and good to say so. His phone buzzed. "Then I'll learn the drum part," Paisley replied. Emile grinned, set the phone down, and began the chant again from the first line.

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: When every sentence is about the same length, writing tends to sound monotonous; mixing short and long sentences gives it rhythm.
story:
Mr. Reyes had read Kayla's story aloud on Friday, and by the third paragraph Rex had put his head down on his desk like a man surrendering. Nikola had yawned twice, which for Nikola was a lot, since she usually stayed awake even during the fire drills. Kayla sat at the kitchen table on Sunday with the draft in front of her, a red pen in her hand, and the beginnings of a grudge.

The story itself was fine. It was about a dog that stole a whole birthday cake and blamed the cat, and Kayla did not think the plot was the problem. She read the first paragraph out loud to the empty kitchen, quietly, so her mother wouldn't ask questions. Each sentence trundled along, and then the next one trundled the same distance, and then the one after that. She tapped her pen against the table at the end of every sentence and noticed something: the taps came evenly, like a metronome.

She tried an experiment, because experiments felt more logical than sulking. She read the paragraph again and counted the words in each sentence on her fingers. Sixteen. Fourteen. Fifteen. Seventeen. Sixteen. She wrote the numbers in the margin. They were all about the same length, every single one, and hearing them read aloud was like walking down a hallway with evenly spaced doors, none of them leading anywhere surprising. That was the trap. When every sentence was about the same length, the writing sounded monotonous. She had built a perfectly even hallway and then made people walk down it.

Her dilemma was that she liked her sentences. They were long and polite and full of words like "very" and "really" and "beautiful," which she'd been told since third grade were good words. She underlined the weak ones anyway. "Very big" could just be "enormous." "Really pretty" could be "gleaming." "Suddenly and quickly" could be a single word, or possibly nothing, since the dog was already moving at speed. The cuts felt rude, like telling guests to leave a party, but each one made the remaining words work harder.

Then she calibrate-tested the rhythm, in her own way: she read the new version aloud and tapped her pen again. Sixteen. Two. Nine. Fourteen. Three. When she hit the two-word sentence, she actually laughed, alone, at her kitchen table, which she decided not to examine too closely. The short ones landed like doorways opening sideways. The long ones had room to carry details. Mixed together, the paragraph had a rhythm you could walk to, or at least stroll.

On Monday she handed in the revision, and Mr. Reyes read the first page aloud. At the two-word sentence, Rex lifted his head off the desk. Nikola mouthed "enormous" back at her with an approving eyebrow. At the part where the dog framed the cat, somebody in the back row said "no way," which was more commentary than her first draft had received all period.

Mr. Reyes set the pages down. "Same story?" he asked.

"Same story," Kayla said. "Different hallway."

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience.
story:
Samantha taped a strip of masking tape across the living room rug and wrote LEFT on it in marker. The radiator behind the couch continued to radiate heat into the room, even though her mother had turned the thermostat down an hour ago, and Samantha wiped her forehead with her sleeve.

"Again," she said to Muhammad and Viviane, who stood beside her on the rug, facing the couch as if it were an audience. "Ms. Nasser said we exit stage left after the second song, and we only get one run-through backstage before the concert."

Viviane looked down at her feet. "So left is, like, the piano side? Where the curtains are?"

"Left from where?" Samantha said. "That's the whole problem. If I'm facing the couch and Muhammad's facing the window, my left and his left point opposite ways."

Muhammad spun to face the window, then the couch, then the window again, holding out his arms. His left hand pointed at the bookshelf one time and the television the next, depending on where he stood. He stopped. "It flips every time you turn around," he said. "So whose left is it?"

Samantha thought about the diagram Ms. Nasser had sketched on the whiteboard, and about how the arrows on it had seemed backwards to her at first. She turned to face the couch, which was the audience, and raised her own left hand. "Stage left means our left, when we're facing the audience," she said. "The performers' left. Not the audience's."

They practiced it eleven times, walking off past the bookshelf with their backs to the couch.

The night of the concert, the gymnasium lights went hot and bright, and the principal's introduction made the whole thing feel imminent, as if it were already happening before anyone sang a note. They got through the first song. Halfway through the second, Ms. Nasser raised two fingers, the signal, and Muhammad grinned and started walking toward the piano side, the audience's left.

Samantha caught his sleeve and pulled him the other way. He turned, saw the rest of the choir filing off past the far curtain, and mouthed one word at her: "Concept."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The terminator is the line on a sphere where the lit side turns into the shadow side, the edge where direct light stops reaching.
story:
"Terminator?" Philippe whispered. "Like a robot that shoots lasers?" They were standing in front of a huge painting of a single orange sphere at the city art gallery, and the word had just appeared on Ms. Szabó's worksheet.

"It's not a robot," Marissa said, reading ahead. "On a sphere, the terminator is the line where the lit side turns into the shadow side. It's the edge where direct light stops reaching."

Mia squinted at the painting. The sphere had a bright spot, like a tiny sun trapped inside the orange, and a curved line ran down its middle. Past that line, everything went dark, and an even darker oval stretched across the table beneath it. Her own drawing, tucked under her arm, looked flat as a pancake. That was the whole reason she'd signed up for this sketching session: her sphere drawings kept looking like circles, and Monday's art assignment was mandatory if she wanted to pass the term.

"The sphere is showing off," Philippe said. "Yours is just lying there."

"Thanks." Mia pulled out her sketchbook anyway. If she could isolate that line, the exact place where light quit, maybe the rest would follow. First the bright spot, the highlight. Then the terminator curving around. Then the dark side, and finally the smudged oval on the table, the cast shadow.

She drew the circle. She imagined a flashlight aimed from the upper left, the way the gallery lights hit the actual wall. Where would the light stop reaching? Right about... there. She pressed harder with her pencil on one side of her curved line, then harder still, then dragged her finger across the table for the shadow.

Marissa leaned over. "Whoa. It actually looks round."

"Round-ish," Mia said, but she was grinning. She held the page up next to the painting. "Okay, Mr. Sphere. You win this round."

Philippe raised his pencil like a sword. "The terminator will be back."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Labeling each moving box with the room it belongs in and its contents makes unpacking faster, because boxes can be carried straight to the right place.
story:
The moving truck had left forty boxes on the floor of the new house, and not one of them said what was inside. Asher stared at the stack in the living room, all sealed with brown tape, all exactly the same opaque brown. His mom opened three in a row: pots, books, then a tangle of extension cords. "Where are the sheets?" she asked, because his bed had to be made tonight and nobody knew which box held them.

In his old town, his friend Terry had moved the summer before, and Asher remembered the first night at Terry's new place. Terry had dug through box after box in his pajamas, hunting for his bedsheets while his dad held open flaps and said, "Not that one." They finally found the sheets at the bottom of a box marked kitchen towels. Terry had said, "We should have written where each box goes and what's in it." Asher had nodded, but he hadn't really digested the idea until now, standing in front of forty brown mysteries.

So he tested it. While his mom searched, he grabbed a marker and a pad of sticky notes and went to the boxes she had already opened. POTS, he wrote, KITCHEN. He carried the pot box straight to the kitchen himself and set it on the counter, no sorting needed. It took him ten seconds. Then he did it with the books: BOOKS, MY ROOM, and up the stairs it went. His mom stopped rummaging and watched him. "Do the rest," she said. "Any box we open, it gets a note."

They opened boxes together after that, calling out contents, and Asher labeled each one with its room. The sheets turned up in box twenty-six, but by then it hardly mattered, because every opened box had already gone where it belonged and the living room floor was clearing fast. He made his bed and slept without the cold feeling he had braced himself for.

The next morning was his first day at the new school, and Mr. Campbell stood at the door of the classroom shaking hands. "You must be Asher," he said. Two kids near the window looked over, and one of them, a girl with a braid, raised a hand and waved. Asher walked toward the empty desk beside her and said, "Hi, I just moved here. I'm still figuring out where everything goes."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Benjamin sat at the computer with two news tabs open and a notebook page torn nearly in half from erasing. Both stories were about the same poll, the one about the dilapidated gym roof at school and whether the town should pay to fix it. One story said support had gone from 40 percent to 50 percent. The other said support had jumped 25 percent. He read them twice more, then leaned back until the chair creaked.

"Charlie," he typed into the chat window, "how can the same poll be ten and twenty-five at the same time? Somebody's lying."

"Maybe the second reporter can't do math," Charlie wrote back. "Or the first one is asleep. Pick one."

Benjamin wasn't satisfied with either. He opened the school's sports page next, because that always calmed him down, and found Mr. Moretti's article about the basketball team's season. The team's shooting had improved, the article said, by 25 percent since December. He checked the stats table himself: December, 40 percent from the field. February, 50 percent. There it was again. He sat very still, the way he did when a pattern was hiding somewhere just out of reach.

He grabbed a pencil. Ten out of a hundred, that was the rise he could see. But ten sat on top of forty, not a hundred. He wrote 10 over 40, then 25 over 100, and stared at them until they matched. The two numbers weren't fighting. Ten was the raw climb; twenty-five was the climb measured against where you started. "Percentage points," he said out loud to the empty room, trying the phrase on. "That's the ten."

He went back to the chat. "They're both right," he told Charlie. "Ten points and twenty-five percent. Same change, two names."

"That's annoying," Charlie wrote.

"Extremely," Benjamin agreed.

The next morning he found Mr. Moretti by the gym office, holding a clipboard and a mug with a chip on the rim. Benjamin showed him both articles on his phone. "Your story says ten, the other one says twenty-five," he said. "Which do we put in the school paper?"

Mr. Moretti studied the screen. "Which one tells the truth faster?"

"Ten, if you already know the numbers. Twenty-five, if you want the jump to feel big."

"Then print both," Mr. Moretti said, and penciled something on his clipboard. "Side by side. Let the reader do the arithmetic."

That afternoon Benjamin sat at the computer again, cursor blinking in an empty document. He typed the headline, deleted it, retyped it, and hit print. Charlie was going to hate it, which meant it was probably good.

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: The darker a roux is cooked, the less it thickens, because browning breaks down the flour's starch.
story:
Kate stood behind the folding table at Ms. Hughes's market stall, gripping a wooden spoon like a sword. Ms. Hughes sold cheese sauce over roasted potatoes every Saturday, and today she had promised to teach Kate how to make it, because Kate wanted to surprise her dad on his birthday. He still talked about the lumpy gravy from last Thanksgiving, and Kate had sworn that would never happen again.

"Flour and butter first," Ms. Hughes said. "That paste is called a roux. Then milk, then cheese. Smooth as a river." She was called away to the register, so Kate stirred while her classmate Leonardo, who had wandered over with quarters for honey sticks, watched the pan. "Can I try?" he asked, and before Kate could answer, he had the spoon. He loved watching things turn golden, so he stirred and stirred, hypnotized, until the roux went the color of caramel, then the color of an old penny. When Kate got the pan back, she whisked in the warm milk, added the cheese, and stirred. The sauce refused to thicken. It ran off the spoon like watery juice.

"Did we add enough flour?" Leonardo asked, peeking into the pan as if the answer were submerge at the bottom. Kate thought hard. She remembered her dad's gravy last fall, pale and gluey, thick as wallpaper paste. Same amount of flour as today, she was almost sure, but hers had been white when it went in. The sauce here had gone thin only after Leonardo cooked the roux dark. She tested the idea the only way she could: she started a fresh batch, kept it pale blond, and poured in the milk. Within a minute, the sauce clung to the spoon in a glossy ribbon. She looked at the penny-colored pan beside it and laughed. "The darker a roux gets, the less it thickens. You cooked our thickener away."

"You mean the pretty part was the problem?" Leonardo said, wounded. "That's betrayal." Ms. Hughes came back, dipped a spoon in the new sauce, and nodded. "Nice save, you two." The suspense of the birthday dinner suddenly felt lighter, and Kate ladled the sauce over a test potato. Leonardo took the first bite, closed his eyes, and held up his honey stick like a torch. "Your dad," he announced, "is going to cry."

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Mandarin Chinese, zuǒ means left and yòu means right, each said with its own tone.
story:
Raphael stood on Dexter's front porch with his phone in his hand and a plan he had been building for three days. He was going to find the noodle shop on Fenwick Street by himself, and he was going to ask for directions in Mandarin, because last summer he had refused to try even one word.

That memory still sat in his chest like something corrosive, eating at him whenever he thought about it. His grandmother had walked him to the market that summer, pointing left and right, teaching him two small words over and over. He had shrugged and mumbled and pretended not to care, and she had gone quiet for the rest of the walk. Now she was back for a visit, and he wanted to show her something.

"Zuǒ means left," Dexter said, holding the door open. "My grandma says it all the time. And yòu means right. They don't sound the same either. Zuǒ goes down at the end, like you're dropping something. Yòu goes up, like a question." Dexter's little brother Cedar ran past with a water gun, shouting both words in the wrong tones, and Dexter rolled his eyes.

"But they're each said with their own tone," Raphael said slowly, trying it out. "So if I get the tone wrong, I might say the wrong thing entirely." He frowned. That was the hidden part. The words weren't just sounds; they were sounds riding on pitches, and the pitch was doing half the work. He said zuǒ out loud, letting his voice sink, then yòu, letting it lift. Cedar shouted "ZOO-oh!" from the yard, dropping his voice so hard it sounded like a dying robot, and Dexter laughed so hard he had to lean on the doorframe.

Raphael decided to test it before he left. He asked Cedar to point when he said each word, using only the tones to know which was which. He said zuǒ, low and falling, and Cedar pointed left. He said yòu, rising, and Cedar swung his finger right. He said zuǒ again and got left again. It was working. The tone really was carrying the meaning, like a second set of words hidden inside the first.

At the corner of Fenwick Street, an old man was sweeping outside a bakery. Raphael's heart hammered, but he stepped forward. "Qǐng wèn, zuǒ háishi yòu?" he asked, dropping his voice on the first word and lifting it on the second, exactly as he had practiced. The man raised his eyebrows, then pointed right, and said something that ended in a clear, rising "yòu."

Two blocks later, Raphael found the noodle shop, steam fogging the window, the smell of broth drifting out onto the sidewalk. He bought two containers, one for his grandmother and one for himself.
