On the walk home he kept repeating both words under his breath, low and high, low and high, so he would still have them when she opened the door. "Zuǒ and yòu," he said to nobody. "Left and right."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
story:
Hazel had twenty dollars of birthday money in her pocket and one goal: new basketball shoes. The old ones had a hole by the left toe, and tryouts were in two weeks. At the mall entrance, a huge screen showed a pro player spinning a ball on one finger while wearing silver HighGlide shoes. "The choice of champions," the caption said. Behind her, a girl around her age was telling her mom that literally everyone at school already had HighGlides.

Tiana caught up with her near the fountain, out of breath. "Tell Paul to hurry. He's still looking at the sneaker wall like it's a museum."

"It kind of is," Hazel said. They joined Paul in front of a display where a poster shouted "Don't be the last one left in boring shoes!" Hazel frowned at it. "That poster is doing something to us."

"Doing what?" Paul asked.

She pointed at the poster, then at the screen near the entrance, then at a cardboard cutout of the famous player. "The screen says a star wears them, so we trust them. The poster says everyone has them, so we feel left out. And 'boring' is a loaded word. It's not describing the shoes, it's describing us if we don't buy them." She had learned the pattern from a library project about wartime posters. While digging through old posters, she had found something better: a group that had worked on exactly this problem. "The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda," she told Tiana and Paul, reciting it the way she had for her presentation. "Ordinary people. That's the whole point. You don't have to be a genius to spot the trick."

"So what do we do, a science experiment in the shoe store?" Tiana said.

"Actually, yes." Hazel counted the tricks on her fingers. "Celebrity, bandwagon, loaded words. My test: if an ad gives me zero facts about the shoe itself, it's probably hiding something." She turned over a HighGlide box. The writing was vague and ambiguous, all "revolutionary feel" and "next-level energy," with nothing about cushioning or durability. Then she picked up a plain box from the bottom shelf. It listed the materials, the support, and a lower price.

Mr. Li, who ran the shop, came over with a stool for Tiana's tired little brother, who had been wobbling on one foot by the stroller. "Kids your size grow out of shoes fast," he said. "The flash sells, but the plain ones hold up." He tapped the plain box. "And this week they're two dollars off."

Hazel tried them on and jumped twice. Good grip, no pinching. Paul held up the silver HighGlides one last time, then set them back. "Twenty dollars more for a famous fingerprint," he said. "I despise being advertised at."

"Same," said Tiana. "Well. Mostly."

At the register, Hazel paid for the plain shoes and still had change left. On the way out they passed the giant screen again, the champion still spinning his ball. Hazel waved at it like an old acquaintance. "Nice try," she said.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
Alexandre kept one eye on the basketball game and one on the trivia sheet folded in his pocket. Between quarters, his school ran a contest, and the winner got courtside seats for the final. Skyler had beaten him in every trivia round this year, and Alexandre wanted this one. The problem was the last question, the one worth double points: "What is the maximum NFL passer rating?" Abbey leaned over from the next seat, munching popcorn, because Abbey only came to basketball games to argue about football.

"A hundred," Alexandre said. "Perfect has to be a hundred, right?"

Abbey shook her head slowly, the way she did when she was about to enjoy being right. "My uncle says it's the weirdest number in sports. He won't disclose it, either. He says I have to earn it." She pulled out her phone, showed a screenshot of a stats page, then covered half of it with her thumb, keeping her expression neutral so Alexandre couldn't tell whether the answer was hiding under her thumb or not. The gym smelled like rubber floors and popcorn butter, and the scoreboard buzzed as the second quarter ended.

Ms. Johansson, who taught math and kept score at every home game, paused in the aisle with her clipboard. Alexandre asked her the question before he could stop himself. She smiled but shook her head, pointing at the contest rules like a doctor refusing to hand over a prescription without an exam. "You can look it up after the buzzer," she said. "Not before."

The third quarter started, sneakers squealing, and Alexandre couldn't focus on it. Skyler had scribbled "100" on his sheet with a smug little shrug. A perfect score being something other than a hundred felt wrong, and that wrongness itched at him. If Skyler guessed 100, Alexandre needed the strange number. He thought about how the scoreboard compressed four quarters into one final score, how a single number could hold a whole game inside it. Maybe a passer rating squashed several stats together, and maybe squashed numbers didn't land where you expected. He wrote 158.3, half guessing, half reasoning, and slid the sheet to the judge.

When the winner was announced at the final buzzer, the judge read his answer aloud. "Correct, one hundred fifty-eight point three." Abbey uncovered her thumb, revealing the same number on her screenshot. "My uncle says it's a perfect game," she said. "Go enjoy your seats."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Havdalah ceremony uses a cup of wine or grape juice, fragrant spices to smell, and a braided candle with several wicks.
story:
Gavin had been waiting for Saturday evening all day, because his cousin's house was hosting the Havdalah ceremony and, for the first time, he was old enough to be trusted with a job. When the sky finally went dark, his aunt poured a small cup of grape juice and set out a little silver holder full of fragrant spices. Then she handed Gavin the braided candle. It had several wicks twisted together, and when she lit it, the flames bent toward each other in a way that made him lean closer. His little sister reached for it, and he pulled it back, careful. "It's the Havdalah candle," his cousin Lindsay said from across the table. "Everybody gets to smell the spices."

Gavin wanted to do more than just hold the candle, though. He wanted to know why the spices were there at all. You could see the flame and taste the juice, but a smell was invisible, and he wondered if it had something to do with the day of rest ending. He devised a test. During the singing, when nobody was watching him closely, he covered the spice holder with his hand and took a slow breath through his nose. Then he uncovered it and breathed in again. The sharp, sweet smell rushed into his nose so strongly that his eyes watered, and he understood without anyone telling him: the smell was the whole point, something you were supposed to notice with a part of yourself you couldn't see.

Later, while his cousin Lilianne passed around pieces of honey cake, she asked him what he thought of his first real job. "I think the protagonist of tonight was me," Gavin said, and then went red, because that had come out louder than he meant. Lilianne laughed, but not in a mean way. "You held it like it was authentic," she said. "Like a real one from a real family."

The house emptied slowly, coats and goodbyes and one last slice of cake for the road. When only the paper plates were left, Gavin's sister tugged his sleeve. "Next time," she whispered, "can I hold the candle?" Gavin looked at the twisted wax, still warm in his hand, and set it carefully back in its box with her name written on a sticky note.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
Marcus rang Lyam's doorbell with the controller already in his pocket. Today was supposed to be the tournament. They had planned it all week at lunch, eight players, Krish bringing the snacks, the bracket drawn on graph paper in Marcus's backpack right now. Lyam opened the door only halfway, which was strange, because Lyam never did anything halfway.

"Not today," Lyam said. "Just go home."

"Go home? You drew the bracket." Marcus held up the paper, but Lyam was already looking back into the house, toward the kitchen, where his mother's voice was low and quick.

"I don't feel like it. Forget it." The door shut. Not slammed, exactly, but close enough that Marcus felt the air move past his face.

He stood on the porch for a while. Ants had colonized the crack between the bottom step and the walkway, streaming in and out, and he watched them only because he didn't want to watch the door. Lyam was spontaneous, the kind of kid who once started a water fight in January. He didn't cancel things. Unless, Marcus thought, he'd just been pretending all along, the kind of person who dumps you the second something better shows up. That felt true, standing there. It felt true all the way across the street, where Mr. Chaudhry was watering his roses, and Marcus was so busy deciding what kind of person Lyam was that he barely heard Mr. Chaudhry say, "Terrible thing this morning. Did you hear about the dog?"

Marcus stopped. "What dog?"

"Lyam's. The brown one, Biscuit. Car, right out front, before school. His dad drove them to the vet an hour ago." Mr. Chaudhury shook his head and went back to his roses.

So that was it. Not Lyam's personality, not some secret plan, just a terrible morning that Marcus had walked into the middle of. On the bus home, he put one earbud in and let the podcast queue run. A host was talking about a psychologist named Lee Ross, who in 1977 had called it the fundamental attribution error, the way people blame someone's actions on their personality while missing the situation they're in. Marcus rewound it twice. He had done it today, in under a minute, on a porch.

He texted Krish to cancel the snacks, then walked back to Lyam's house and rang the bell again. Through the door he heard slow footsteps, then the latch.

"I'm not playing," Lyam said.

"I know. I just came to say Biscuit was a good dog." Marcus held out the bracket. "And this can wait as long as you want."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The darkest part of a cast shadow is right where the sphere touches the surface, because almost no light can reach into that narrow gap.
story:
Max slid his drawing across the picnic table so Yohan could see it. "It's a sphere," Max said, "with the light coming from up there, like Ms. Ong set it up." He had shaded the curve carefully, leaving a bright highlight on the upper left and a soft shadow along the lower right, exactly the way the demo ball looked on the wooden stool.

Yohan tilted his head at the page. "It's good, but it's kind of floating. Like a planet." He held the drawing next to the real setup, where a baseball sat on the stool under the camp's one bright lamp. "The ball looks stuck to the stool. Yours looks like it's hovering an inch above the table."

Max frowned and compared them side by side. The shapes matched. The shading matched. He squatted down until his eyes were level with the stool, staring at the place where the ball met the wood. Right at the point of contact, there was a ring of almost pure black, so dark it looked like a drawn line. Farther out, the shadow on the stool faded to gray. He hadn't noticed it from above, but down here it was obvious. He grabbed his softest pencil, the 6B, and pressed a small dark crescent exactly where sphere touched surface, then let it fade outward.

"Whoa," Yohan said when Max held the drawing up again. "It dropped! It's sitting on the table now." Max laughed out loud. A counselor walking past asked what all the noise was about, and Max said, "The darkest part of a cast shadow is right where the sphere touches the surface." He said it like he was announcing a score.

By the next afternoon, half the art shed wanted to know the trick. Bronson had been struggling all week with an orange that looked airborne, and he petitioned Ms. Ong to move the whole still-life table closer to the window so everyone could study their own contact points. Ms. Ong agreed, on one condition. "Each of you draws two spheres," she said, "one with the light from the left, one from the right, so you can see what changes."

Max set up fast, pencil already sharpened. He drew the first sphere with its dark crescent tucked against the surface, then started the second one, mirroring the light. "This one will be perfectly symmetrical to the first," he told Bronson, "except flipped. Highlight moves, shadow moves, but the darkest spot stays where the ball touches." Bronson leaned over, watching Max press the pencil down into that same magic spot. "That," Bronson said, "is the best floating orange fixer I've ever seen."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
Juliette had made forty-one free throws in a row at practice on Tuesday, and now her left elbow throbbed with every dribble. She stood at the foul line in the gym, rubbing the joint while Katelyn rebounded for her.

"You're holding your elbow again," Katelyn said, tossing her the ball. "Yann says you do it every time you miss."

"I'm not missing." But she was, and she knew it. The pain had started three weeks ago, right after Coach had run those drills where the whole team shot a hundred layups a day. She'd loved those drills at first, loved watching her percentage climb, feeling the improvement almost like a visible thing. Now she wondered if she'd been reckless, piling shot after shot onto an arm that was still growing.

She thought about her little brother's baseball league. Last spring their mom had dragged the whole family to his game, and the pitcher, a tall kid named Danny, got pulled in the fourth inning even though he was winning. "Pitch limit," the other parents had grumbled, and Danny's dad had shrugged and said, "Growth plates. They're areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones, and they're weaker than the bone around them." Someone added that it was why young athletes had limits on repetitive stress. Juliette had barely listened, half asleep in the bleachers. She listened now.

She had a theory, anyway. She stopped shooting, walked to the bleachers, and sat down. "I'm testing something," she told Katelyn. "Three days of no shots, just running and passing. If it's the repetition doing it, my elbow should quiet down."

"You're going to look like a quitter," Katelyn said.

"Watch me not care."

Ms. Weiss, the gym teacher, noticed her sitting out on Thursday and raised an eyebrow, but Juliette only passed and drove and defended, and by Friday the throb had faded to almost nothing. She stood at the foul line again, alone after practice, and bounced the ball twice.

"Okay," she whispered to her elbow. "Forty-one was plenty."

She rose up and shot.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently

fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
story:
Sloane's garage smelled like solder and burnt cheese crackers, and the robotics club had been arguing for twenty minutes. "Digby died at the fair because the battery drained," Frank insisted. "It can't consume power that fast unless the motors stalled." Sloane shook her head. "The code looped. I watched the log. The wheels didn't even twitch." Nolan had been standing near the table, where Digby sat with his sensors intact but his emergency light still blinking red, and he kept thinking about the toxic smell he'd noticed right before the shutdown, sharp and chemical, like a leaking battery.

Mr. Torres, whose house backed onto Sloane's yard, had left a note taped to the garage door that morning. Sloane read it out loud: "Heard your robot quit at the fair. Before you fight about it, look at the book on my porch. Borrowed it from the library years ago and never returned it. Old story. Might help. T." On the porch sat a fat paperback of tales from ancient India, and inside, a parable about blind men and an elephant. Each man touched one part. One felt the trunk and called the elephant a snake. Another felt the leg and said it was a pillar. Another felt the ear and swore it was a fan. Nolan read it twice, then carried the book back inside.

"Guys. We're the blind men," he said, and laid the book open on the workbench. "Frank touched the battery. Sloane touched the code. I smelled the leak. Nobody touched the whole elephant." So they tested it. Sloane ran the log again while Frank measured the cells and Nolan checked the air sensor. The power was fine. The code was fine. The air sensor had detected fumes and triggered the emergency shutdown.

"That means Digby didn't fail," Sloane said slowly. "He did exactly what we built him to do."

Frank grinned and pulled the fair results sheet from his backpack, folded into quarters. He smoothed it flat on the table and pointed to a line halfway down the page, and there, in the judge's neat printing, was Digby's name under Safety Award, First Place.

"He got a ribbon," Frank said. "Our robot has a ribbon and we spent a week mad at him."

Nolan laughed and clipped the fresh battery in place. "Sorry, Digby. Now let's go be blind about something new."

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: A motif is an image, object or idea that keeps recurring through a literary work, and tracking where it reappears helps a reader see what it comes to mean.
story:
Mackenzie had turned the corner of her reading nook into a detective's office. The window seat held her novel, a stack of pink sticky notes, and a mug of cocoa going cold. On page after page she pressed a pink note wherever the old lighthouse lantern appeared, because her teacher had called it a motif, and Mackenzie had formulated a plan: mark every page, then line them up and see what the lantern was really doing in the story.

At first the lantern seemed like decoration. It lit the harbor, it hung in the keeper's window, it flickered during storms. Marcel had said so at school on Friday. "It's just a lamp," he'd insisted. "A lamp that shows up a lot."

"A motif is an image or object or idea that keeps recurring through a book," Mackenzie had told him, tapping her copy. "And if I track where it comes back, I can see what it comes to mean." Marcel had shrugged, but Karter leaned over and asked if she would show him her notes on Monday.

Now it was Sunday afternoon, and the sticky notes were spread across the nook like a pink tide. Mackenzie counted eighteen of them. She arranged them in order, chapter by chapter, and read her own labels aloud in a whisper. Chapter three: lantern keeps the ships safe. Chapter nine: lantern in the granddaughter's window when she is afraid. Chapter fourteen: lantern dark because the keeper has died. Chapter nineteen: the granddaughter lights it herself.

She sat back against the cushion. The lantern was not about lamps at all. Early in the book it meant being watched over; by the end it meant doing the watching over. Same object, new meaning, and she could see the change only because she had followed it page by page. It was like her nightly ritual of checking the lock on the back door before bed, the same small act that meant something different once she was the last one awake.

Monday at recess she spread the notes along the cafeteria table. Karter walked his finger down the row and stopped at chapter nineteen. "Wait," he said. "So the granddaughter becomes the keeper?"

"That's the twist," Mackenzie said. "The lantern doesn't change. Who holds it does."

Marcel picked up the sticky note from chapter fourteen, the dark one, and turned it over in his hands. "Huh," he said. "So it was never just a lamp." He reached into his backpack and pulled out his own novel and a pad of yellow sticky notes. "Show me where to start."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
Eleanor set her fork down perpendicular to her plate, which was how she arranged things when she was thinking, and stared at the two columns of numbers she had copied onto a napkin. "Dad, can I ask you something that is not about dinner?" Her dad said sure, as long as she ate her green beans while she asked. She had until eight o'clock tonight to message Ms. Pritchard with her doubles partner for Saturday's table tennis tournament, and the whole choice hinged on one number that she was starting to distrust.

"Rowan and Pearl both average twelve points a game," she said. "Exactly the same. But watch." She read down the napkin. Rowan's games went eleven, twelve, thirteen, twelve, twelve, eleven. Pearl's went nineteen, three, twenty, four, eighteen, four. "If I just tell Ms. Pritchard the average, they look like the same player. They're not the same player at all." The numbers had colonized her brain since last period, spreading until she couldn't think about anything else, and now she had proof on a napkin that the average was hiding something.

Her dad leaned over and read the columns, chewing his beans. "So which one do you want?" That was the real question, and Eleanor realized she hadn't answered it yet, only proven that it needed answering. Rowan had already texted her three times saying please pick me, I've been practicing my serve every day, so Eleanor knew how much Rowan wanted this. And Rowan was steady, which felt safe. But Eleanor kept picturing Saturday as a knockout bracket, where you lose once and you're done. In that kind of tournament, terrible games end you, but spectacular games win you trophies.

She tried a test out loud, tapping the napkin with one finger. "If Pearl plays like her good games, we win the whole thing. If she plays like her bad games, we're out in the first round. Rowan never does either. Rowan just plays." Her dad said, "Sounds like you already know what you're trading." She did. She picked up her phone and typed the message to Ms. Pritchard, then put the phone face down between her fork and her knife, still perpendicular, still thinking.

Before she could exhale, Rowan's reply buzzed through the table: "any news?" Eleanor looked at the napkin one last time, then typed back, "Can I tell you tomorrow? I picked Pearl, and I want to explain why face to face." She pressed send, folded the napkin into her pocket, and ate her green beans.
